
{{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|image=Amanotanagao shrine torii - 2010.jpg|caption=[[Torii]] gate and Haiden}}'''Amenota Nagao Shrine''' (Ame no Tanaga Ojinja,<ref name="日本廻国記">『日本廻国記 一宮巡歴』 pp.278-281</ref><ref name="日本歴史地名大系">『日本歴史地名大系 43 長崎県の地名』 pp.814-815</ref><ref name="長崎県の歴史散歩">『長崎県の歴史散歩』 p.202</ref> Amanotanaga Ojinja <ref name="日本廻国記一宮表">『日本廻国記 一宮巡歴』 p.294</ref> <ref name="別冊歴史読本">『別冊歴史読本 7 諸国一宮と謎の神々』 p.150</ref> <ref name="完全ガイド">『日本全国 一の宮巡拝完全ガイド』 p.139</ref> ) is a Shinto shrine in Iki City, Nagasaki Prefecture. It is a [[:en:Myōjin Taisha|Myōjin Taisha]] and the [[Ichinomiya]] of Iki Province.
Although people think the Shrine was listed in the "[[Engishiki Jinmyōchō]]", the evidence supporting this claim is not very convincing.
==History==
According to 'Munakata Taisha' ('Fukuoka Prefecture'), in 'Munakata Daibosatsu Goengi', during 'Empress Jingū''s 'Sankan Seibatsu', the Grand Minister of Munakata ('the deity of Munakata Taisha') attached two red and white flags to a pole called 'Mitenaga' held by 'Takenouchi no Sukune'. By raising and lowering this pole, they confused the enemy and finally planted it on 'Iki no Shima' ('Okinoshima (Fukuoka)' in 'Genkai Sea'). The name 'Amatenaga-no-Mikoto Shrine' ('Ame-no-Tenaga-no-Mikoto') is said to have originated from this 'Mitenaga'.
In 'Konin 2' (811), the shrine was founded under the name 'Ameno-Tanaga-o Shrine' (天手長雄神社), later becoming 'Amatenaga-no-Mikoto Shrine'. According to 'Dai Nihon Koku Ichinogu-ki' ('"Ichinogu-ki"'), 'Amatenaga-no-Mikoto Shrine' and 'Amatenagahime Shrine' were located in 'Monobe Village (Nagasaki)', and 'Amatenaga-no-Mikoto Shrine' was considered the 'Ichinomiya' ('First Shrine') of Iki Province.<ref name="大日本地名辞書"/> In 'Ichinogu-ki', the enshrined deity was 'Omoikane'.<ref name="別冊歴史読本"/><ref name="群書類従">'Gunsho Ruijū, Volume 2, Shinto Section', p.246</ref>.
Later, the shrine declined due to the 'Mongol invasions of Japan', and its location became unknown.
The current 'Amatenaga-no-Mikoto Shrine' was identified during the 'Edo period' by 'Tachibana Mitsuyoshi', a 'kokugaku' ('national scholar') of 'Hirado Domain'. Before this, the shrine was a small sanctuary known as 'Wakamiya'. Mitsuyoshi associated it with the ancient shrine of 'Myōjin Taisha' ('Amatenaga-no-Mikoto Shrine') due to the local place name 'Tanakao' ('Tanaka-o'). Entering the bamboo grove of 'Tanaka Castle Hill', he unearthed a sacred mirror and two stone statues of 'Maitreya'. He then built a stone shrine to house them. One of the Maitreya statues, discovered in 'Enpō 5' ('1677'), bore an inscription from 'Enkyū 3' ('1071') and was later designated an 'Important Cultural Property'. As of 2012, it is preserved in the 'Nara National Museum'.<ref name="長崎県の歴史散歩"/><ref>[http://www.narahaku.go.jp/collection/958-11.html Important Cultural Property | Maitreya Seated Statue (Discovered at Hachigamine Sutra Mound, Nagasaki Prefecture) | Nara National Museum] (Accessed February 1, 2012)</ref>. In 'Genroku 1' ('1688'), the 'Matsuura Domain' lord ordered the construction of a shrine building.
Mitsuyoshi's method of identifying 'Shikinaisha' ('shrines listed in the 'Engishiki') was largely based on place names, which modern research questions. Regarding 'Amatenaga-no-Mikoto Shrine', there is a theory that the true shrine is 'Kō Shrine (Iki)' in 'Yutake-Okoshi', 'Ashibe Town'. The name 'Kō' ('興') is thought to mean 'Kōfu' ('国府', meaning provincial capital), and since the shrine grounds also contain the 'Sōja' ('Sōja', the shrine representing all shrines in a province), it is widely believed that Kō Shrine is the true 'Amatenaga-no-Mikoto Shrine', and thus the true 'Ichinomiya' of Iki Province. However, Mitsuyoshi mistakenly identified 'Kō Shrine' as 'Yo Shrine' ('與神社'), likely misreading the characters.
The 'Amatenagahime Shrine' that was merged into the current shrine was also designated by Mitsuyoshi, but its original location remains unknown. Similarly, 'Monobe Futsu Shrine' was identified based on the fact that 'Tanaka Fure' ('田中触') was part of 'Monobe Village'. However, modern research suggests that the true 'Monobe Futsu Shrine' was likely 'Kunitsu Shrine (Iki)' in 'Wataraura'. During the 'Heian period', 'Moribe District (Iki)' existed in this region, and later included the areas corresponding to 'Monobe Village' in the Edo period and the present-day 'Tanaka Fure' and 'Wataraura'.<ref>'Kadokawa Japan Place Name Dictionary 42 Nagasaki Prefecture', p.951</ref>.
Regardless of these historical uncertainties, the current shrine is recognized as the 'Ichinomiya' of Iki Province, enshrining both 'Amatenagahime' and 'Monobe Futsu' deities.
